1 Abstract
This thesis examines how the parliamentary representation of smaller parties is affected by the transi-
tion from Hagenbach-Bischoff to Double Pukelsheim. To do so, all 31 available cantonal parliamentary 
elections for the eight transition cantons between 2007 and 2026 are analyzed. The smaller parties 
groups, combines all electoral lists and parties which received less than 10% of the total votes in the 
analyzed area. To make this comparison, the offical results under Double Pukelsheim are taken and 
the counterfactual seat allocation under Hagenbach-Bischoff is computed. This while including the 
former canton electoral law and holding electoral units, observed votes, seat totals and reported list 
structures constant.
The main finding is that across all 31 elections, the smaller parties aggregately receive a 7.6 percentage 
points higher seat-share under Double Pukelsheim than under the conterfactual Hagenbach-Bischoff. 
An aggregate gain for the smaller parties occurs in 30 of 31 elections. Further is the observed gain 
persistent to alternative smaller-party thresholds, across succesive elections and to the omission of 
individual cantons. While analyses regarding the pre-reform district magnitude or explicit electoral 
thresholds, reveal no consistent relationship, respectively are sensitive to the inclusion of individual 
cantons.
The persistent mechanical seat-share gain for smaller parties observed here, indicate the reduction of 
the prior representational disadvantage under the Double Pukelsheim system. This while behavioural 
responses to the reform remain outside the scope of the analysis.

3 Introduction
On the 18 December 2002 the Swiss Federal Supreme Court (FSC) came to a conclusion, which 
disrupted the Swiss Electoral System. In BGE 129 I 185 the FSC criticized that in the elections for the 
Council of the City of Zurich, the thresholds for parties to win a seat varied heavily from district to 
district. Further did some districts have thresholds for parties to win a seat of up to 34%. Consequently, 
votes did not have equal effect, which undermines the electoral equality included in Art. 8 (Equality 
before the law) and Art. 34 (political rights) of the Federal Constitution. Based on this criticism the 
court decided that the City of Zurich had to implement corrective measures, but could choose their 
form (BGE 129 I 185 E. 7.3, E. 7.6.2–7.6.3 and E. 8.3.2; Schweizerische Eidgenossenschaft, 1999, Arts. 
8 and 34). The Government of the Canton of Zurich decided to keep the constituency structure and 
instead commissioned the german mathematician Friedrich Pukelsheim to develop a comprehensive 
and at the same time minimally invasive solution for the problem. Eventually Pukelsheim came up 
with a method called “biproportional divisor method with standard rounding” which is today often 
simply called “Double Pukelsheimer” or “Biproportional apportionment”. (Regierungsrat des Kantons 
Zürich, 2014, pp. 3–4; Lüscher, 2024, pp. 9-10)
The distinguishing feature of the Pukelsheimer Proporz to other proportional representation systems, 
is the so called upper-apportionment. It artificially creates a single electoral district for the initial allo-
cation of the parliamentary seats to the parties or list groups. Through this mechanism, the difference 
between seat and voteshares gets minimized and with that also the effective threshold for parties to 
enter the parliament. (Lüscher, 2023, p. 575)
Through its upper-apportionment mechanism and the lowered threshold, the reform is especially 
relevant for the representation of smaller parties, since votes that would previously have been ineffec-
tive in small constituencies can now contribute to a seat gain at the cantonal level. Sandro Lüscher 
illustrates this mechanical effect with the case of Schwyz’s Landrat election in 2016, there under the 
old Hagenbach-Bischoff system, the Green Liberal Party would not have won a single seat, whereas 
under the new method they received three seats (Lüscher, 2025, p. 1-3).
Since Zurich first used the system in 2007, eight further cantons have used it: Schaffhausen (2008), 
Aargau (2009), Nidwalden (2014), Zug (2014), Schwyz (2016) , Valais (2017) , Uri (2020), Graubünden 
(2022). In 2025 also the voters from Basel Landschaft decided to implement the biproportional 
apportionment from 2027 on (Lüscher , 2024, p.17 ; Kanton Basel-Landschaft, 2025a, p.7 ; Kanton Basel-
Landschaft, 2025b) While nine of these cantons already implemented the algorithm, more cantons are 
currently discussing the implementation too. In Thurgau, the initiative “Mehr Transparenz bei Wahlen 
im Thurgau” is currently pending at the Grand Council of the Canton and a special parliamentary 
committee is examining the iniatitive, also in the canton of Lucerne, the iniatitive “Faire Wahlen ohne 
Listenflut” was submitted and the voters will be able to decide on the effectuation (Grosser Rat des 
Kantons Thurgau, n.d.; Regierungsrat des Kantons Luzern, 2026, pp. 19–20). In the canton of St.Gallen 
in 2026 an initiative to adapt the Pukelsheimer algorithm was launched (Initiativkomitee «Damit jede 
Stimme zählt», n.d.).
The amount of cantons who have already implemented the system or are debating about doing so, 
suggests that the decision by the FSC had a substantial impact on how Swiss citizens elect their 
regional parliaments today. It seems that the double-Pukelsheimer through its wide implementation

across cantons is a success story. Since the first election under double Pukelsheim in Zurich in 2007, 
the system has been used in 32 cantonal parliamentary elections.1
Taken together, this number of elections and almost 20 years of experience provide a reason to evaluate 
the impact of the reform, especially on smaller parties. How much has the reform changed smaller 
parties’ seat shares and how large is the actual difference in seat allocation between the Hagenbach-
Bischoff and Double Pukelsheim system? Are there other major differences, for example based on the 
pre-reform district sizes and how do smaller parties seat shares evolve across successive elections?
Existing research primarily examines Double Pukelsheim in legal, normative, or system-level terms. 
A few studies also conduct counterfactual comparisons, but these cover either individual elections 
or only one election per canton (Pukelsheim & Schuhmacher, 2011, pp. 1590–1592; Leuzinger, 2018, 
p. 42; Lüscher, 2024, p. 13). Although their results indicate that smaller parties can benefit from Double 
Pukelsheim, the magnitude and consistency of this mechanical allocation difference across successive 
elections remain less systematically examined.
This thesis addresses this gap by applying a consistent Hagenbach–Bischoff counterfactual to 31 
elections in eight transition cantons. Two Graubünden elections are presented as contextual compar -
isons but excluded from the main transition estimate. Holding the observed post-reform votes and list 
structure constant, the analysis measures the difference in the share of seats won by smaller electoral 
lists and examines variation across institutional settings and successive elections.

4.1 Institutional and Theoretical Background
This chapter provides the institutional and theoretical background for analyzing the transition from 
Hagenbach-Bischoff to Double Pukelsheim and reviews the relevant literature. It first outlines the 
historical development of electoral systems in Switzerland and then explains the functioning and 
limitations of the Hagenbach-Bischoff and Double Pukelsheim methods. It subsequently examines 
the adoption and canton-specific implementation of Double Pukelsheim. Finally, the literature review 
situates this thesis within previous research before the expected effects of the transition are derived.

4.1.2 The Hagenbach-Bischoff Method
To be able to comprehend later the differences between the HB and the DP Method one has to 
understand the allocation under the priorly used Hagenbach-Bischoff system.
Under Hagenbach-Bischoff, seats are allocated separately in each constituency. Let 𝑀 denote the 
number of mandates in the constituency, 𝑣𝑖 the votes for an eligible list 𝑖, and 𝑉  the total list votes 
used to calculate the distribution number. Whereas the distribution number 𝐷 is the smallest integer 
strictly greater than 𝑉 /(𝑀 + 1). In the first allocation, each list receives the integer part of its votes 
divided by 𝐷 (Bundeskanzlei, 2025, p. 41):
𝐷 = ⌊ 𝑉𝑀 + 1⌋ + 1, 𝑠𝑖 = ⌊𝑣𝑖𝐷⌋.
If the first allocation leaves seats unassigned, the remaining seats are awarded one at a time. For each 
list, its votes are divided by the number of seats it currently holds plus one. The list with the highest 
quotient receives the next seat; its quotient ℎ𝑖 and the allocated seats 𝑠𝑖 are then recalculated, and the 
process continues until all 𝑀 seats have been filled:
ℎ𝑖 = 𝑣𝑖𝑠𝑖 + 1.

It should be noted, that the HB system calculation produces the same allocation as the D’Hondt divisor 
method with downward rounding (Bundeskanzlei, 2025, p. 41). Further there are some factors, like list 
alliances, eligibility thresholds, and rules for resolving equal quotients which depend on the electoral 
law of the corresponding canton. The counterfactual in this thesis applies the relevant former cantonal 
rules within each constituency, as detailed in the Data Cleaning section.
The central weakness of the traditional cantonal application of Hagenbach–Bischoff does not arise 
solely from the allocation formula, but from applying it separately in constituencies that often have few 
seats. Small district magnitudes create high and across districts varying natural thresholds, meaning 
that votes for smaller parties may fail to contribute to a seat.This might hinder equality of electoral 
success and systematically disadvantage smaller parties. As shown in the later section on the adoption 
of Double Pukelsheim, these inequalities were central to the legal and political debates that led several 
cantons to adopt Double Pukelsheim. (Pukelsheim & Schuhmacher, 2004, pp. 507-508, 521; BGE 129 I 
185 E. 7.1.1 and E. 7.6.2)
4.1.3 The Double Pukelsheimer Method
Based on the weaknesses of the Hagenbach-Bischoff Method and the FSC decision, the canton of Zurich 
comissioned the mathematician Friedrich Pukelsheim to develop a new method (Lüscher, 2024, p.10). 
The following section explores how the algorithm works and how it makes sure that it complies with 
the Federal Law and mitigates the HB weaknesses.
Based on Article 8 and 34 of the Federal Constitution, there are three dimensions of electoral equality, 
which have to be followed. These are principle of equal voting value, equality of voting power and 
equality of electoral value. The equal voting value ensures that each voter within an electoral district 
gets allocated the identical number of votes. The second principle is the equality of voting power 
(voting weight guarantee). This requires the population represented per seat to be approximately equal 
across electoral districts. Thirdly there is the equality of electoral success, which should assure, that 
all votes contribute equally to the election and that as many votes as possible are taken into account in 
the allocation of seats. (Pukelsheim & Schuhmacher, 2004, pp. 506-507) Districts with fewer than nine 
seats have a natural quorum above 10% under the approximation 1/(𝑀 + 1), where 𝑀 is the number 
of seats. The Federal Supreme Court treats 10% as a target for natural quorums when redesigning 
an electoral system. Exceptionally, compelling historical or regional minority-protection reasons may 
justify a higher natural quorum. (Pukelsheim & Schuhmacher, 2004, p. 505; BGE 131 I 74 E. 5.2–5.4) 
Equality of counting value concerns the formal treatment of votes, while equality of voting power 
depends on the separately determined ratio of population to seats in each electoral district (Pukelsheim 
& Schuhmacher, 2004, pp. 507, 515–516). For the traditional application of Hagenbach–Bischoff, the 
main difficulty lies in equality of electoral success when small districts impose high natural thresholds 
(Pukelsheim & Schuhmacher, 2004, p. 508; BGE 129 I 185 E. 7.1.1 and E. 7.6.2).
To approach this main issue of the Hagenbach-Bischoff, the Double Pukelsheimer or originally called 
the “Neues Zürcher Zuteilungsverfahren” knows a upper and a lower apportionment (Pukelsheim & 
Schuhmacher, 2004, p.513).
• Upper Apportionment To bypass the natural quorums, in the upper apportionment, the whole 
canton is seen as one single district. All the seats are then directly proportionally to the vote share 
allocated towards the parties. For that the votes from the district-level have to be summarized on a 
4

cantonal level. This leads to the first difficulty, which arises through the variation in district magni-
tude and the resulting circumstance that voters receive across constituencies a different amount of 
votes. Therefore to be able to summarize the votes on a global level, the number of votes have to be 
translated, which is done as described followingly. The number of party votes per constituency are 
taken and divided with the respective number of seats. The resulting quotient gets rounded to the 
next number and indicates the amount of voters per list. The rounded quotients, can then be summed 
across all districts and divided by the cantonal divisor to get each parties total seats. The divisor 
itself is set by an official authority, in Zurich for example, its the Department of the Government 
Councillor which is responsible for the elections. The responsible authority, needs to assure that 
with the chosen divisor exactly as many seats can be allocated as there are available. The number of 
seats which result per party, are rounded again to the next number. (Pukelsheim & Schuchmacher, 
2011, p.1584-1585 ; Kanton Zürich, 2003, § 10 and 103)
• Lower Apportionment This part of the apportionment process, assigns each party’s cantonwide 
seats from the upper apportionment to its district lists while preserving each district’s predetermined 
seat total. First, the party votes in each district are divided by a district divisor chosen so that the 
rounded results add up to the district’s seats (Pukelsheim & Schuhmacher, 2011, p. 1585). These initial 
allocations may not match the parties’ cantonwide entitlements: in the 2011 Zurich election, the SVP 
would have received 55 seats instead of the 54 assigned in the upper apportionment . To correct such 
differences, every district list of a party is divided by the same additional list group divisor. A divisor 
above one reduces the party’s unrounded quotients and can remove seats while a divisor below 
one can add seats. (Pukelsheim & Schuhmacher, 2011, p. 1586) This effect can be illustrated with 
a hypothetical numerical example based on the 2011 seat mismatch for the SVP mentioned above. 
Now it could be that the SVP list in District Y would have a quotient after division by the district 
divisor of 2.51. With the standard rounding, the SVP would receive three seats in this district. But if 
now as a list group divisor 1.01 is taken, then this quotient falls to 2.51/1.01 ≈ 2.49, and the SVP 
would get allocated only two seats in this district. Through that the mismatch would be resolved, 
considering that in no other district, the allocated number of seats for the SVP would drop too. If this 
is the case, then instead of 1.01 a smaller divisor would had to be choosen until, only the amount of 
seats fall away, which are needed. Further might the change in District Y cause, that the district gets 
allocated one seat less then it should have. The party and district divisors are then adjusted in turn 
until every party receives its cantonwide entitlement and every district retains its fixed number of 
seats. (Pukelsheim & Schuhmacher, 2011, p. 1586)
To summarize, the upper apportionment in the Double Pukelsheim system reduces inequalities in 
electoral success caused by the high natural thresholds of small constituencies under the previous 
district-by-district Hagenbach-Bischoff system. It does so by pooling parties votes across the canton 
before seats are assigned to constituencies. This is also the main improvement of DP regarding the 
three dimensions of electoral equality in contrast to Hagenbach-Bischoff.
4.1.3.1 Trade-offs and Criticisms
Alike every proportional system, also the Double Pukelsheimer system has its flaws for which it gets 
criticized. One of the main weaknesses of the biproprtional apportionment compared to the HB System 
is its complexity. It gets mentioned throughout, that its relatively difficult to understand the system 
holistically and that there is profound knowledge needed, to be able to compute the seat allocation. 
5

(Bundeskanzlei, 2013, p. 19 ; Bundeskanzlei, 2025, p.24 ; Lüscher, 2024, p.20) Lüscher tough mentions, 
that the usage of list alliances under the priorly used Hagenbach-Bischoff method also led to a high 
complexity situation. This especially since, beforehand the election it was impossible to estimate, 
which party would profit from the alliance. (Lüscher, 2024, p.20) Another main point of criticism, are 
the so called “discordant seat allocations”. The discordant seat allocations describe the phenomena 
when within a district a party gets allocated more seats than another party with more votes in that 
district. This phenomena can appear through the lower apportionment process and the dual role of 
the system to achieve proportionality both on cantonal and district-level. The emerging situation, 
can cause confusement and frustration especially within the party which received more votes in that 
specific constituency. (Pukelsheim & Schuhmacher, 2004, p. 519) Not only for the parties themself it 
can be irritating, but also for the voters. This especially since in Switzerland elections often contain a 
personal vote component. If then a popular figure from one party, loses its seat to a less known figure 
from another party and district, this may raise concerns and lower the acceptance of thee system. A 
reaction to this flaw of the DP-System, was that the cantons of Zug, Schaffhausen and Graubünden 
implemented a majority clause, which aims to ensure that the strongest list in the corresponding 
constituency receives atleast one seat. (Lüscher, 2024, p. 21) Friedrich Pukelsheim was already aware 
of this issue in 2004 and pointed out that the so called majority requirement can in rare ocassions be 
not fulfilled. On base of this he mentioned the possibility of the implementation of such a majority 
clause. (Pukelsheim & Schuhmacher, 2004, p. 520) Another issue of the system, is that different turnout 
level and different proportions of residents who are eligible to vote in the consituencies can determine 
the allocated mandates of other constituencies. To illustrate this, Lüscher provides an example: There 
are three Districts with the same size and number of mandates, but while District 1 produces 50% of all 
votes, District 2 and 3 only produce each 25%. Through this District 1 determines 50% of the canton-
wide party result, while only having 33.3% of the mandates. Subsequently this leads to under- and 
overrepresentation in the corresponding districts. (Lüscher, 2023, pp. 578-579) One other point which 
was often discussed to be a possible weakness of the Double Pukelsheim, is a possible Party System 
Fragmentation. For example both reports of the Swiss Federal Chancellery in 2013 and 2025 mention 
the possible party fragmentation in parliaments. As a possible measure to prevent fragmentation, 
the implentation of thresholds is mentioned. (Bundeskanzlei, 2013, p.18 ; Bundeskanzlei, 2025, p. 24) 
Despite this concerns, Sandro Lüscher came in his Thesis to the perception, that the general trend of 
a rising amount of parties in swiss cantonal parliaments, is unrelated to the implementation of the 
Double Pukelsheim. He then also mentioned, that the inexistency of an effect, might come from that 
several cantons have implemented the by the Federal Chancellerey mentioned thresholds. (Lüscher, 
2024, p. 135) Therefore it can’t be conclusively stated, whether the reform would have had an impact 
on party system fragmentation without the implentation of thresholds or not.
Taken together, these criticisms illustrate the central trade-offs of Double Pukelsheim. Although the 
system improves canton-wide proportionality and reduces the number of ineffective votes, it does 
so at the cost of greater computational complexity and potentially counterintuitive outcomes at the 
constituency level. Electoral thresholds can mitigate discordant seat allocations and party-system 
fragmentation, but may simultaneously weaken proportionality. The system therefore does not elim -
inate electoral distortions entirely, it rather prioritizes party proportionality and equal vote success 
over simplicity and fully autonomous constituency-level representation.

4.1.4 The Adoption of Double Pukelsheim in Swiss Cantons
In the following paragraphs the arguments brought up in each reform canton will be discussed in 
chronological order. The year in the beginning of each entry, marks the year of first application of the 
double Pukelsheimer in the corresponding canton.
• 2007: The canton of Zurich as the initiatior of the development of the Double Pukelsheimer 
Algorithm, became the first canton to make use of it in 2007. The reform followed a 2002 voting-
rights complaint about elections to Zurich’s city parliament. The Swiss Federal Supreme Court 
partially upheld the complaint. It found that the thresholds in some districts with up to 33.3% were 
massively above the 10% threshold, which is seen as compatible with the prinicples of proportional 
representation. Further was it claimed, that thresholds vary to much between districts. The ruling 
required the city of Zurich to reform its electoral system, subsequently the canton of Zurich, which

party competition and vote distributions vary between elections. This institutional variation motivates 
the exploratory comparisons below: whether smaller parties seat-share gains differ by the presence of 
an explicit quorum, and across successive elections within the same canton.
4.2 Literature Review
Building on the institutional mechanisms described above, the existing empirical literature generally 
finds that Double Pukelsheim improves vote–seat proportionality and benefits parties that were 
disadvantaged by small electoral districts. However, the studies differ substantially in their research 
designs, geographical coverage, and treatment of counterfactual electoral rules.
Pukelsheim and Schuhmacher provide an early counterfactual comparison based on the 2011 Zurich 
election. They apply the former Hagenbach–Bischoff method to the observed votes while assuming 
four hypothetical list alliances based on political orientations and historical alliances. Under this 
counterfactual, the larger SVP, SP, and FDP receive additional seats, primarily at the expense of smaller 
parties such as the BDP and Alternative List. Their calculation also indicates considerably greater 
inequality in the electoral success of votes under Hagenbach–Bischoff. The analysis nevertheless 
concerns only one election, and its results depend partly on assumptions about which list alliances 
parties would have formed. (Pukelsheim & Schuhmacher, 2011, pp. 1590–1592)
Lüscher conducts a similar comparison for the 2016 Schwyz election. Under his Hagenbach–Bischoff 
counterfactual, which does not assume any list alliances, the dominant SVP and CVP would have 
benefited. Whereas the left alliance and especially the GLP benefited from the implementation of the 
Double Pukelsheim. Most notably, the GLP’s three observed seats would have been reduced to zero 
under Hagenbach–Bischoff. (Lüscher, 2024, p. 13) This example illustrates the potentially substantial 
effect of the allocation rule on an individual smaller party, but it does not establish whether effects of 
this magnitude occur systematically across cantons and elections.
Leuzinger broadens the comparison by examining the most recent election in each of the seven cantons 
that had introduced Double Pukelsheim by 2018. His study is the closest precedent for the present 
analysis because it calculates hypothetical seat distributions under the former cantonal electoral 
systems. However, it covers only one election per canton and assumes that the list alliances observed 
in the final pre-reform election would have persisted (Leuzinger, 2018, p. 42). The present thesis does 
not carry these historical alliances forward. Consequently, the two counterfactual specifications can 
produce different Hagenbach–Bischoff seat allocations. This illustrates the sensitivity of counterfactual 
results to assumptions about unobserved alliance formation. Leuzinger also mentions that he observed, 
that mainly smaller parties profited from the transition and that around 10% of the mandates mechan-
ically change the party, through the transition (Leuzinger , 2018, p.42).
Taken together, the counterfactual calculations by Pukelsheim and Schuhmacher, Lüscher, and 
Leuzinger constitute the closest methodological precedents for the present thesis. They apply a former 
allocation rule to votes observed under Double Pukelsheim and compare the resulting counterfactual 
seat distribution with the actual allocation. Their comparisons therefore hold the observed post-reform 
vote distribution constant and isolate the difference produced by the allocation rules.
The interpretation of this difference can be clarified using Fiva and Folke’s framework for separating 
the mechanical and psychological effects of electoral reform. Fiva and Folke examine a reform of 
Norwegian municipal elections, first applied in 2003, that replaced D’Hondt with modified Sainte-
11

Laguë. (Fiva & Folke, 2016 , p.266) Their principal estimate of the mechanical reform effect compares 
the actual pre-reform allocation with a counterfactual application of the new formula to the same 
pre-reform votes. They also apply the former and new formulas to the same post-reform votes to 
examine how behavioral responses may alter the magnitude of the mechanical effect. (Fiva & Folke, 
2016, pp. 270–272) The Swiss studies described above, and the present thesis, follow this latter compu-
tational approach: the former formula is applied counterfactually to votes observed under the new 
system. This measures the mechanical allocation difference conditional on the observed post-reform 
vote distribution, but it does not estimate how parties and voters would have behaved had the former 
system remained in place or identify the reform’s complete causal effect.
Rather than recalculating individual elections, Lüscher’s principal empirical analysis estimates how 
cantonal political outcomes would have developed without the reforms. He finds that Double 
Pukelsheim substantially reduced vote–seat disproportionality, with stronger improvements in can -
tons that previously had smaller average district magnitudes (Lüscher, 2024, pp. 129–143). However, 
Lüscher finds no significant increase in the effective number of parliamentary parties or electoral can-
didacies. Voter turnout initially declined slightly, but this effect diminished over subsequent elections. 
These findings distinguish the reform’s immediate mechanical consequences from its more limited 
behavioural effects on parties and voters.(Lüscher, 2024, pp. 143–145)
The existing literature therefore provides strong evidence that Double Pukelsheim improves propor -
tionality, as well as several examples in which smaller parties gain seats. What remains less systemat-
ically examined is the magnitude and consistency of the conditional mechanical allocation difference 
across successive elections. Existing counterfactual studies either focus on individual elections or cover 
only one election per reform canton, while Lüscher’s analysis examines aggregate disproportionality 
and broader political outcomes rather than the election-specific seat gains of smaller parties.
This thesis addresses that narrower gap by applying a consistent Hagenbach–Bischoff counterfactual 
to 31 elections in eight transition cantons. Two elections from Graubünden are additionally presented 
as contextual comparisons. Because Graubünden previously used majority voting rather than Hagen-
bach–Bischoff, these allocations are hypothetical and are excluded from the main transition estimate. 
The thesis holds observed post-reform votes constant, applies a common definition of smaller parties, 
and measures their change in seat share for every election. In contrast to Leuzinger (2018) and 
Pukelsheim & Schuchmacher (2011), it does not assume that hypothetical or historical pre-reform 
alliances would have persisted. The analysis therefore estimates the mechanical allocation difference 
conditional on the observed votes without introducing an additional behavioral assumption about 
counterfactual alliance formation.
4.3 Expected Effects of the Transition
Based on the theoretical considerations developed in the preceding sections, several effects can be 
expected from the transition of the Hagenbach–Bischoff method to the Double Pukelsheim system. 
Under a district-by-district Hagenbach–Bischoff allocation, small district magnitudes create high 
natural thresholds for winning a parliamentary seat. Votes for parties which fail to win a seat in a 
district, won’t contribute elsewhere. This produces ineffective votes and therefore disproportionately 
disadvantages smaller parties. The biproportional apportionment instead through the upper appor -
tionment pools votes across the whole relevant area, before it distributes each party’s seats among the 
12

districts. This should increase the equality of electoral success and reduce vote–seat disproportionality. 
Therefore mechanically, and conditional on the same observed votes, smaller parties that surpass the 
applicable legal thresholds are expected to receive a larger seat share under Double Pukelsheim, while 
the seat advantage previously enjoyed by larger parties should decline (Pukelsheim & Schuhmacher, 
2004, pp. 506–508, 513-514 , 518).
The magnitude of this mechanical difference should depend particularly on district magnitude under 
the Hagenbach–Bischoff comparison. The fewer seats allocated in a district, the larger the vote share 
a party generally needs to obtain mandates. Double Pukelsheim should therefore produce larger gains 
for smaller parties where the former or counterfactual Hagenbach–Bischoff allocation consists of 
many low-magnitude districts than where seats are already allocated in relatively large districts. This 
expectation is consistent with Lüscher’s finding that the reduction in disproportionality was stronger 
in cantons with smaller pre-reform average district magnitudes (Lüscher, 2024, pp. 132–133).
The effect is also expected to depend on the specific institutional design adopted by each canton. 
Reflecting Switzerland’s federal structure, the reformed cantons differ in their use of canton-wide 
and district-level legal thresholds, majority clauses, and other supplementary adjustments. Explicit 
electoral thresholds can restrict gains among smaller parties by excluding lists that do not reach the 
required vote share and can therefore partly offset the greater proportionality produced by the upper 
apportionment (Bundeskanzlei, 2013, p. 18; Lüscher, 2024, pp. 107, 135). The majority clause on the 
other hand as no direct effect on the smaller party seat-share gain. Since the cantons ensure in their 
law, that the seat entitlements according to the upper apportionment hold. Zug’s law for e.g. explicitly 
states that the majority clause gets deactivitated if it is essential to fulfill the upper apportionment seat 
entitlement. (Kanton Schaffhausen, 1904/2019, Art. 2d para. 1bis and 2(b); Kanton Zug, 2006/2026, § 
52e para. 1a, 1b and 2(b); Kanton Graubünden, 2021/2026, Art. 28 para. 2 and 4(b))
Valais and Uri are particularly important special cases because Double Pukelsheim does not cover the 
canton through a single canton-wide upper apportionment. Valais conducts separate upper apportion-
ments in six electoral regions, so votes aren’t pooled across the entire canton. This is expected to limit 
the proportionality-enhancing effect relative to a fully canton-wide implementation, particularly for 
parties whose support is dispersed across regions (Lüscher, 2024, p. 57). In Uri, Double Pukelsheim 
applies only to the four biggest muncipialities, while the remaining ones use Majorz. This limits the 
territorial and numerical scope of the reform, although it does not necessarily reduce the mechanical 
effect among the four municipalities included in the upper apportionment (Kanton Uri, 2019, pp. 4, 
10–11; Lüscher, 2024, pp. 64–67).
Comparisons across successive elections also provide exploratory context by examining whether 
smaller parties’ mechanical seat-share gains persist or vary over time. No directional trend is hypoth-
esized, as vote distributions, the composition of the smaller-party group, and electoral rules can change 
between elections
The estimated difference may additionally depend on the electoral rules used to construct the counter-
factual outcomes, including the treatment of list alliances and canton-specific allocation provisions.
Together, these expectations provide the foundation for the following hypothesis and exploratory 
questions concerning differences in smaller parties’ seat shares.

tual Hagenbach-Bischoff allocation vary between elections conducted with and without an explicit 
electoral quorum?

An explicit quorum is a legally specified minimum vote share that a party or list group must reach 
at at a district or cantonal level to qualify for seat allocation. Among the eight cantons of the main 
analysis, five have applied an explicit quorum. Whereas Aargau is a special case, since it implemented 
the quroum only from the second election under Double Pukelsheim on. The canton of Graubünden 
implemented an explicit quroum and is shown for context. Further details around the details of the 
implementation of explicit thresholds across the cantons are stated in Section 4.1.4. Unlike the natural 
threshold created by limited district magnitude, the explicit quroum directly excludes parties that do 
not satisfy the legal requirements.
Because such quorums may prevent smaller parties from benefiting from the pooling of votes under 
Double Pukelsheim, the following directional expectation is formulated:
On average, the gain in smaller parties’ seat share under Double Pukelsheim relative to 
the counterfactual Hagenbach-Bischoff allocation is smaller in elections with an explicit 
electoral quorum than in elections without one.
This comparison is interpreted descriptively because the level and geographical application of the 
quorums differ across cantons and elections and coincide with other institutional differences.
5.2.3 Exploratory question 3: Change across successive elections
How does the gain in smaller parties’ seat share under Double Pukelsheim relative to the counterfactual 
Hagenbach-Bischoff allocation evolve across successive elections within each canton?
This analysis extends Hypothesis 1 by following the seat shares under both allocation rules and their 
difference Δ𝑒 from each canton’s first election under Double Pukelsheim onward. It assesses whether 
the overall difference identified in Hypothesis 1 is persistent across elections or driven by particular 
election-specific outcomes.
Stable positive values of Δ𝑒 would indicate a persistent mechanical advantage for smaller parties, 
whereas substantial fluctuations or changes in sign would suggest that the effect is strongly dependent 
on the circumstances of individual elections. The within-canton perspective further provides a clear 
separate image for each canton, without mixing their different electoral systems. Given that the smaller 
parties seat share, the party composition, aswell as the district magnitudes and electoral rules can 
change between elections, no directional trend can be hypothesized.
6 Research Design and Analysis
6.1 Research Design and Counterfactual Strategy
This thesis uses a deterministic counterfactual reallocation design. The main analysis covers all 31 
cantonal parliamentary elections held under Double Pukelsheim in Switzerland through 2026 in the 
eight cantons in which Hagenbach–Bischoff previously was in use as the electoral system. The two 
elections from Graubünden are included as contextual comparisons since the canton had previously 
used a majority voting system. At the computational level, the observations are electoral lists within 
electoral constituencies and elections, while the primary unit of comparison is the election.
Each election is evaluated under two allocation regimes. The observed outcome is the official allocation 
under Double Pukelsheim, obtained from the relevant cantonal election authority. The counterfactual 
outcome is obtained by applying the specified former legal allocation rules to the same election’s 
16

observed votes, electoral units, seat magnitudes, and reported list structure. Each election therefore 
serves as its own comparison.
The counterfactual is constructed in five steps.
First, the official election files are imported and standardized to obtain, for every election, electoral 
unit, and reported list or list group, the observed votes, seat magnitude, and official Double Pukelsheim 
seats. Party and list labels are harmonized across source files, and voter numbers or vote shares are 
reconstructed where not already directly published by the structure of the official data.
Second, the counterfactual inputs are defined by holding the observed votes, electoral units, seat 
magnitudes, and reported list configuration constant. Joint lists reported as one unit in the official 
results remain pooled while lists affiliated with the same party, but running independently remain 
separated.
Third, the specified former allocation regime is applied separately within each electoral unit. Most 
counterfactual allocations use the district-level Hagenbach–Bischoff method described above. Where 
the former cantonal rules contained additional rules such as, quoruoms, majority-clauses, or tie-
breaking provisions, these are incorporated into the calculation. The applicable canton-specific rules 
and features are documented in Section 6.2.
Fourth, the counterfactual seats obtained in the individual constituencies are aggregated to the party-
election level and merged with the official Double Pukelsheim seat totals.
Finally, the resulting datasets are validated by checking party coverage, vote and seat consistency, 
electoral-unit seat totals, and the total number of seats allocated under both regimes. Where the source 
data provide multiple measures of the official Double Pukelsheim result such as upper-apportionment 
totals, lower apportionment totals, reported list mandates, or elected-candidate counts these measures 
are additionally reconciled. If exact ties between parties occur, they are if possible resolved with the 
applicable former cantonal laws. For the two cases in which the tie persisted, both possible seat alloca-
tions were presented for the affected parties. This assures, that a seat is never assigned unintentionally 
through e.g. the arbitrary ordering of rows. The two mentioned unresolved alternatives were observed 
in Graubünden 2022 and Schwyz 2024 and concern only parties above the 10% threshold and therefore 
do not affect the main smaller-party comparison.
The resulting contrast between the observed Double Pukelsheim allocation and the countrefactual is 
interpreted as a mechanical allocation difference conditional on the observed post-reform votes and 
not as the reforms complete causal effect. This since these votes were cast under Double Pukelsheim 
and the analysis cannot determine how voters, parties, number of candidates, campaign strategies, or 
list alliances would have differed if the former electoral regime had remained in force.

Across the nine reform cantons, the counterfactual applies a district-level allocation to the electoral

Beyond the statutory allocation rules, the counterfactual requires an assumption about unobserved 
list alliances. Unlike Leuzinger and Pukelsheim & Schuhmacher, this analysis does not carry historical 
or hypothetical alliances forward. List alliances are in this thesis seen as strategic and election-specific 
rather than fixed institutional parameters. This leads to, that election-specific, historical alliances 
cannot simply be assumed to persist across subsequent elections with different parties and vote 
distributions. In Zurich, for example, the last Kantonsrat election under Hagenbach–Bischoff took 
place in 2003. Assuming that the alliances formed in 2003 would still have applied in 2023 despite 
two decades of changes in the party system would therefore introduce a strong and unverifiable 
behavioural assumption. Some parties that formed list alliances in Zurich in 2003 no longer existed or 
contested the 2023 election. Conversely, parties such as the Green Liberal Party, which contested the 
2023 election, did not yet exist in 2003. (Statistisches Amt des Kantons Zürich 2003, table 3; Statistisches 
Amt des Kantons Zürich 2026; Grünliberale Partei Kanton Zürich n.d.). Therefore the counterfactual 
preserves joint lists or list groups represented as a single unit in the observed election data. But it 
does not reconstruct historical alliances or assume new alliances between separately reported units. 
This provides a transparent counterfactual that holds the observed electoral configuration constant 
and estimates the mechanical allocation difference between the specified election-specific regimes.
The exclusion of unobserved list alliances is an important limitation of the counterfactual. Under 
Hagenbach–Bischoff, list alliances can pool votes during seat allocation and thereby improve the 
chances of representation for smaller lists (Pukelsheim & Schuhmacher, 2011, p. 1590). If the parties 
observed under Double Pukelsheim would have formed such alliances under the counterfactual HB 
regime, excluding them may understate smaller parties’ counterfactual HB seat totals and consequently 
overstate their estimated gain under Double Pukelsheim. However, neither the composition of these 
hypothetical alliances nor the distribution of any resulting seat gains can be reliably determined. 
Alliance gains could accrue to larger partners or leave the aggregated representation of parties 
below the 10% threshold unchanged. The direction is therefore theoretically plausible but cannot be 
quantified uniformly across elections.
A second research-design choice concerns the electoral units and their seat magnitudes. In most can -
tons, the reform retained the former territorial districts or municipalities, meaning that the observed 
electoral units broadly correspond to those previously used under HB. The principal scope deviations 
are addressed in the special-cases callout below. Regarding the district magnitudes, the use of election-
specific magnitudes is deliberate. District seat entitlements are generally based on population and 
periodically recalculated. Consequently, the magnitudes from the last pre-reform election would not 
necessarily have remained applicable in later elections even if Hagenbach–Bischoff had been retained. 
The counterfactual therefore holds each observed election’s electoral units and seat magnitudes 
constant across the two regimes. It asks how the same votes would have been translated into seats 
under the former district-level rules, conditional on the contemporary distribution of seats among 
districts.

6.4 Measures and Analytical Strategy
The analyzed_area comprises the whole canton except in Uri, where it covers only Altdorf, Bürglen, 
Erstfeld, and Schattdorf, the four municipalities using Double Pukelsheim. These municipalities 
account for 37 of the canton’s 64 parliamentary seats. The variable seats_allocated_dp records the 
number of seats covered by the comparison, while parliament_size records the full size of the cantonal 
parliament. These values are equal in all analyzed cantons except Uri.
For the purposes of this thesis, a smaller party is defined as an electoral list or list group with a vote 
share below 10% in the analyzed area. Youth lists and other affiliated lists are treated as separate 
analytical units whenever they enter the official Double Pukelsheim allocation separately. Accordingly, 
the term party refers to the standardized electoral list or list group recorded in the dataset and does 
not necessarily correspond to a broader organizational party family. Smaller parties  are identified 
separately for each election using their observed vote shares. The same set of smaller parties is then 
used when comparing the two seat allocations within that election.
The main analysis compares the combined seat shares of smaller parties within each election. For 
this purpose, the seats of all lists below the 10% vote-share threshold are summed separately under 
Double Pukelsheim and Hagenbach–Bischoff. Each total is divided by the number of analyzed seats, 
24

recorded in seats_allocated_dp, and multiplied by 100 to obtain the corresponding seat share as a 
percentage. This produces one aggregate seat-share difference per election. Using seats_allocated_dp 
as the denominator ensures that the measure refers to the same area as the votes and seat allocations 
included in the comparison.
The election-level outcome is the difference between these two seat shares, denoted by Δ𝑒 and defined 
in Hypothesis 1. Positive values indicate that smaller parties collectively receive a larger seat share 
under Double Pukelsheim while negative values indicate a smaller share. A value of five percentage 
points therefore means that their combined share of the analyzed seats is five percentage points higher 
under Double Pukelsheim. This also means, that a negative or positive aggregate difference, does not 
mean that each included party gains or loses seats respectively.
Hypothesis 1 is assessed using the average seat-share differnce aross all 31 elections. In that analysis 
every elections receives equal weight, which means that cantons with more elections held under DP 
are influencing the average stronger. Since the parliament sizes differ, a supplementary weighted mean 
is added, where elections with a bigger parliament influence the mean stronger. It expresses the total 
net seat gain of smaller parties across the included elections as a percentage of the total analyzed 
seats, giving greater weight to elections with more seats. To better display the variation and typical 
gain, the median ,the first and third quartiles are reported additionally. The main summaries exclude 
Graubünden for the reasons set out in Section 6.2 its observations are presented separately for context.
All three exploratory analyses are descriptive. They examine differences across institutional settings 
and successive elections without isolating the causal effects of individual electoral rules.

7 Discussion
In this paper, the general question: “20 Years of the Double Pukelsheim System in Switzerland: What Is 
the Mechanical Effect of the Transition from the Hagenbach-Bischoff Method on the Seat Distribution 
of Smaller Parties?” was answered in two parts. In the first step, the mechanical effect on the smaller 
parties was examined. Subsequently the study examined which conditions could lead to differences in 
the strength of the mechanical effect across cantons or elections.
Regarding the first step, it was found that across elections the smaller sparties collectively gain seat 
shares under Double Pukelsheim compared to Hagenbach Bischoff. The average aggregate unweighted 
seat-share gain was 7.6 percentage points, further did in 30 of the 31 analyzed elections, the smaller 
parties aggregately receive a higher seat-share. In the Uri 2020 election, no eligible smaller party 
contested, thus no seat-share difference could be observed. The gain also persisted when adapting the 
10% smaller parties threshold to 8% and 12%, and after the exclusion of any single canton. Further was 
it observed, that out of the smaller parties group, the lists with atleast 4% and below 6% across all 
elections profited the most from the transition. The findings in Hypothesis 1 are consistent with the 
idea of the upper apportionment process. It lowers the share of ineffective votes and with that highers 
the equality of electoral sucess. (Lüscher, 2024, p. 3)
This finding matches the observations of the existing literature. Leuzinger states that in his analysis 
across seven elections, smaller parties generally received more seats under the new system (Leuzinger, 
2018, p.42) Also in the by Pukelsheim and Schuchmacher analyzed Zurich 2011 election and in the 
Schwyz 2016 election by Lüscher, did smaller parties profit from the implementation (Pukelsheiim & 
Schuhmacher, 2011 ; Lüscher , 2024, p.13).
38

In the second step, potential differences in the effect according to the different implementation of the 
Double Pukelsheim were examined. First it was analyzed with three measures whether the pre-reform 
district sizes have an impact on the seat-share gain or not. No consistent relationship between the prior 
constituency sizes and the gain for smaller parties was found. This is contrary to the formulated expec-
tation. The expectation was, that in cantons with smaller pre-reform districts, were the high natural 
thresholds impose a greater disadvantage, that there the upper apportionment and it’s cantonwide 
mechanism would have a greater effect. The expectation, was also based on Lüscher’s finding that in 
cantons which priorly had smaller districts, the proportionality had increased stronger (Lüscher, 2024, 
pp.132-133). Thus that the analysis here finds no evidence, is it not contradicting Lüscher’s findings. 
Since an improvement in overall proportionality doesn’t need to have a direct impact on the seat-share 
gain for smaller parties.
A sedond exploratory question, examined whether there is a difference in the mechanical seat-share 
difference between elections held with and without an explicit quroum. The examination here observed 
a higher seat-share gain for cantons without an explicit quroum. This fits the literature, since Lüscher 
and the Federal State Chancellery, both argue that explicit threshold can restrict the gains among 
smaller parties. Through which the greater proportionality achieved through the upper apportionment 
gets partly offsetted (Bundeskanzlei, 2013, p. 18; Lüscher, 2024, pp. 107, 135). Thus of the seen effect in 
the analyis and the support of the theory for an effect, is the effect seen in this thesis analysis sensitive 
to the inclusion of Schaffhausen. This to a point, that without the Schaffhausen elections, the effect 
reverses. Therefore the observed effect needs to be interpreted cautiously.
The third exploratory question analyzes the seat-share gains across sucessive elections within and 
with respect to each cantons electoral rules. Through this approach, it brings together elements of 
the preceding analyses. The results show that the positive seat-share advantage generally persists 
across successive elections, further supporting the main finding. Although average gains are higher at 
later election numbers, mean within-canton changes do not follow a consistently increasing pattern. 
Moreover, fewer cantons contribute to the later comparisons, and some changes are sensitive to the 
inclusion of individual cantons. The findings therefore do not establish that additional elections under 
Double Pukelsheim increase smaller parties mechanical seat-share gain.
In order to analyze all relevant elections and their various underlying assumptions, a few assumption 
had to be made. The analyis, holds all post-reform votes constant and identifies the conditional 
mechanical difference, without capturing the behavioural effect of the transition. For the cantons, in 
which priorly list alliances were allowed, are in this thesis no hypothetical list alliances formed. This 
decision might in the relevant cantons understate the smaller lists representation under the Hagen -
bach-Bischoff counterfactual. Further was each list, which ran independently, treated as a separate 
party, since the Double Pukelsheim algorithm also treats them separately. This decision is especially 
relevant in Schaffhausen, were across multiple elections, several affiliated list such as Youth or special-
interest lists ran. In addition to this decisions, do the limited amount of eight cantons and their different 
electoral laws, limit the extent to which the observed differences in gains can be attributed to a single 
feature.
For cantons considering a transition from Hagenbach–Bischoff to Double Pukelsheim, the following 
can be stated. With 30 of the 31 analyzed elections showing a collective seat-share gain for smaller 
39

parties, the findings suggest that a similar mechanical advantage may arise in other cantons adopting 
DP. However, its magnitude depends on canton-specific circumstances, such as electoral rules, district 
sizes, and vote distributions. Behavioural responses by parties and voters introduce further uncertainty. 
It therefore makes sense for cantons to calculate a hypothetical DP allocation based on their observed 
Hagenbach–Bischoff election results. This allows them to assess the potential mechanical seat-share 
changes while explicitly accounting for their electoral structure and the proposed DP rules.
Further research could extend this thesis in the following ways. With examining how plausible 
counterfactual list-alliances affect the estimated gains. As also with adressing the explicit quroums and 
their possible effects. Specifically it could recalculate each observed election under different electoral 
quroums, ceteris paribus, to isolate their mechanical effect on smaller parties representation.
8 Conclusion
In this paper, I examined the mechanical effect of the transition from the Hagenbach-Bischoff Method 
to the Double Pukelsheim on the seat distribution of smaller parties. The thesis focused on examining 
the seat-share differences between the two systems, for parties with less than 10% vote share. For this 
all 31 elections held by the eight transition cantons from HB to DP were, while holding observed votes 
constant analyzed.
For all held elections, the average unweighted seat-share gain was 7.6 percentage points for the 
aggregate smaller parties group. In 30 of 31 elections, did the smaller parties collectively gain seat-
shares. With the Uri 2020 election being the exception, where no list below the 10% smaller parties 
threshold contested, thus no seat-share difference could be observed. The result of a positive seat-share 
difference, further persisted with alternative cutoffs for the smaller-parties group and when excluding 
individual cantons. This findings therefore descriptively support Hypothesis 1.
The further analysis, explored potential differences between cantons, based on pre-reform district sizes 
and explicit quroums. For the relationship between the pre-reform district sizes and the seat-share 
gain, no consistent pattern could be observed. Regarding differences between elections held with and 
without a quroum, a higher seat-share gain for elections without a quroum was observed. However 
is the observed difference sensitive to individual cantons. Further was it found, that average gains 
persisted and even increased across succesive election numbers, even when individual cantons were 
excluded. However were the average within-canton changes less consistent and sensitive to canton 
exclusions. This pattern doesn’t establish that additional elections under Double Pukelsheim increase 
the seat-share gain.
However is this analysis only focusing on mechanical differences conditional on the canton specific 
rules and on the observed post-reform votes and not estimating the reforms complete effect. This 
paper extends the existing knowledge about the mechanical seat-share gains for smaller parties by 
covering all 31 available elections for the eight transition cantons, including the succesive elections 
within each canton. This enables a wider basis to assess the magnitude and consistency of the smaller 
parties advantage under the Double Pukelsheim.
